Samantha — great questions. I attached an operational playbook (PDF) and a failover matrix (xlsx) that map out the scenarios you listed. High-level notes before the call:

1) Partial control-data partition (single-AZ controlplane loss to subset of DP racks)
   - Detection: sudden increase in controlplane RPC latency + 5% token rejection rate; dataplane heartbeat misses > 3s.
   - Automated action (0–30s): controlplane routes requests to healthy DP nodes, apply prefix caching on surviving nodes.
   - Manual/Runbook (30s–10m): run the containment play (see sheet rows 12–18) — advertise local-only routes, increase batching short-term, promote standby router if BGP peer flaps persist.

2) KV cache warmup and session affinity
   - We use sticky KV warmup where leader-promoted nodes pre-populate hot prefixes during the canary window. Warmup progress is visible via the /v1/metrics/cache_warm_ratio endpoint; target >= 85% after 90s.

3) Egress constraints during DR
   - Default posture: egress through customer-managed NAT + egress proxy in the same region. Failover plan avoids cross-region NAT hairpinning by promoting local egress relays and applying ACLs at the VPC gateway.

I also added telemetry suggestions (CPU/GPU utilization by pod, token latency p50/p90/p99, controlplane RPC latency, KV cache hit ratio, per-route error budget burn).

Please review the PDFs ahead of Thursday. If you can share your preferred SLAs for cutover (RPO/RTO targets) we’ll align the canary windows accordingly.

—Priyom

- Playbook tone: each scenario should have an immediate "triage checklist" (first 5 commands) + escalation matrix + rollback trigger thresholds.

Thanks for the initial materials. A couple of topology-level clarifications from our infra team:

- Are you expecting SR-IOV passthrough on inference hosts or will we use DPDK userspace stack? That changes the approach to telemetry and why we might prefer native NIC offload vs. host-bonding.
- For controlplane-to-dataplane auth we need the exact mTLS cipher list to pre-approve on our firewall (we require FIPS-safe ciphers for our regulated tenant).

Also attaching a short internal checklist we will run pre-cutover.

--Aurora Networking

Aurora team — answers inline: 

- SR-IOV vs DPDK: Our recommended default for Aurora is DPDK for predictable multi-tenant scheduling and to preserve observability hooks. We support SR-IOV for single-tenant, latency-critical lanes but require NIC driver lockstep during rolling updates. I added an "interface decision" appendix to the PDF describing tradeoffs.

- mTLS cipher list: we will ship a FIPS-compatible profile; see appendix B in the playbook with the exact OpenSSL cipher string we use: \"TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256\" (we also support more conservative profiles for your cert boundary; we can provide a pre-approved bundle for firewall testing).

Operational note: during the canary window we recommend the following sequence:
  1) Deploy control plane nodes with canary traffic (1–3% of production tokens) for 15m.
  2) Validate KV warm ratio and route convergence (target thresholds in playbook).
  3) Gradually ramp to 20% while enabling prefix caching warming.
  4) Full cutover if error budget < 0.5% over 1h.

Irene — flagging the cert rotation wait windows for the QA steps you added. Marissa — FYI for contractual SLA alignment during the cutover (Aurora expects 2-hour RTO for a full region failover per their contract draft).

—Priyom
